 Thought the era of CDs had come and gone? How wrong you are. We're seeing a real resurgence in physical media at the moment, and CDs are at the forefront of the trend. Below, I've rounded up a selection of the coolest, most interesting, and most lusted-after models we've spotted recently.
 Shanling's EC Zero ASM is a multitalented portable player that can also cast tunes to wireless speakers or headphones via Bluetooth, rip CDs to USB storage in real time, act as a CD transport for your hi-fi, and double as a DAC for other digital devices.
 Trettitre's Retro Ambient Audio System is the eye-catching result of a successful KickStarter campaign. It combines a turntable and cassette system alongside the CD player, all mounted on your wall in an artistic celebration of physical media.
 For those with deep pockets, Rotel's Michi Q5 is an elite-level CD player and transport DAC with an eye-watering price tag to match. And even though it might never make it to market, I couldn't resist including Panasonic 's portable TV-CD player prototype, which won over our Entertainment Editor with its unexpected, boombox-meets-gogglebox design.

 KEF has cemented its position as the dominant manufacturer of active speaker systems in our 2026 What Hi-Fi? Awards . Its stylish all-in-one designs pack streaming smarts, amplification and wireless capability into a pair of stereo speakers, while delivering a level of sound quality that rivals the very best hi-fi separates alternatives.
 It is a formula that has proven irresistible to our judges this year.
 The highlight is undoubtedly the new premium KEF LS Luxe (£3500 / $4000 / AU$6375), which nabs the 'Best speaker system over £3000' trophy. This standmount package refines the company’s well-proven formula by adding a larger Uni-Q driver array (where the tweeter sits in the throat of the mid/bass unit) and a pebble-shaped cabinet made of BMC (Bulk Moulding Compound) rather than MDF.
 Latest Videos From What Hi-Fi? 
 Watch full video here: 
 Compared to the well-established LS50 Wireless II (£2250 / $2499 / AU$4295), the serial winner in the next price band down, the LS Luxe’s larger Uni-Q array (16.5cm vs 13cm) results in improved dynamics, higher volume capability and deeper bass.
 Add in the newer model’s greater internal volume and better-damped enclosure, and the benefits are obvious, from the increased clarity to the crisper stereo imaging.

 KEF LS Luxe review 
 If your budget doesn't extend that far, we can highly recommend the third of KEF’s Award winners, the LSX II LT (£899 / $999 / AU$1695). These smaller speakers will fit nicely into more modest spaces while retaining much of the well-rounded character we so love from their pricier siblings.
 Triangle’s excellent AIO Twin (£599 / $899 / AU$1799) completes our quartet of speaker systems. These are a fine alternative to the KEF LSX II LT, delivering a front-footed and entertaining sound for a more wallet-friendly price, and takes another win in the 'Best speaker system under £750' category.

 (Image credit: What Hi-Fi?) Our expanding music systems category also includes ‘just-add-speakers’ solutions. We are pleased to report that the quality of such products continues to rise. The main attraction for such systems used to be convenience and a lack of clutter, but in recent years manufacturers have really pushed hard on sound quality.
 Listen to the Roksan Caspian 4G Streaming Pre-Amplifier/Power Amplifier (£6500 / $8250 / AU$13,198) combination, and you would be hard-pressed to find a traditional streamer/amplifier alternative that performs better. It is beautifully made too, and is the first pre/power two-box system we've given an Award to, and it wins the new 'Best hi-fi system over £5000' category.
 Well-established class leaders such as the Technics SA-C600 (£749 / $1299 / AU$1849), the Ruark Audio R610 (£1199 / $1899 / AU$2299), the NAD C 3050 (with MDC2 BluOS-D module) (£1749 / $2449 / AU$3799) and Arcam's SA35 (£2999 / $3299 / AU$6495) all hold on to their Awards at their price bands for another year – making this one of the biggest and most varied categories of the year.

 (Image credit: What Hi-Fi?) We have to give Denon’s D-M41DAB microsystem(£399 / $630 / AU$1139) a special mention too. This little budget micro comes with excellent speakers and has been our go-to entry-level system recommendation for almost a decade now.
 While streaming isn’t built-in, it does feature a CD player, radio and Bluetooth. Build quality is also high. Nothing we’ve come across in all this time has made us question our affection for this modest but surprisingly capable package. It remains a great buy.
 NAD took home the overall systems Product of the Year win last year, but will it hold on to that crown for another year with such strong competition for 2026?  Seeing vinyl everywhere again? Want to see what all the fuss is about?
 Whether you're getting back into the habit after a while or spinning a record for the first time, you'll want a turntable that's easy to set up, easy to use, and, most importantly, sounds great.
 That's where the Sony PS-LX3BT comes in. It wowed us earlier this year for doing so much at such a low price, and thanks to early Black Friday sales, that price just got a whole lot better – it's now £199 on Amazon .
 That's £100 off the launch price, and the lowest price we've seen so far. Plenty of leftover cash to kick-start your record collection!
 Five Stars

 The Sony PS-LX3BT comes from a rich heritage – its predecessor, the PS-LX310BT , sat on our list of the best Bluetooth turntables for a number of years.
 It's finally been knocked off by the PS-LX3BT, which builds on its predecessor with a similar fuss-free design and straight-out-of-the-box functionality. Because it's an automatic turntable, you don't need to fiddle with cartridges or even touch the tonearm – the ‘start’ and ‘stop’ buttons are all you'll need for playback.
 Bluetooth operation is simple enough too, with a large Bluetooth button for pairing, and there's also aptX Adaptive codec support for hi-res streaming up to 24-bit/96kHz to compatible Bluetooth speakers and headphones.
 However you listen, though, the sound quality is top-notch for this price level.
 "There’s very little that’s muddled about how the PS-LX3BT goes about presenting our music, as we move from classic pop through to drum’n’bass and a bit of good old fashioned prog metal," our Sony PS-LX3BT review reads. "We’re taken with just how composed, controlled and well-organised the Sony sounds, marvelling at the effortless cohesion and solidity it brings to the entirety of Michael Jackson’s Bad album."
 The PS-LX3BT brings genuine energy and personality to proceedings, with a good dose of textural insight and punch.
 We only reviewed the Sony PS-LX3BT in April, so £100 off already is quite the bargain. If you're a vinyl newbie, we recommend picking up the PS-LX3BT for £199 at Amazon pronto.

 If you've decided your next speakers will be from KEF, you've already narrowed down from a field of superb choices of the best hi-fi speakers you could buy today. Whether it's down to their aesthetics or reputations, KEF's current speakers are a great choice as this list of five-star reviews shows.
 Choosing which KEF speaker is best for you is the same as choosing any speaker : do you require a standmounter or floorstanding model , what's your budget, do you need passive stereo speakers to go with your existing separates system or are you after a minimal all-in-one wireless speaker system?
 Most of KEF's speakers feature the firm's clever and now-iconic Uni-Q driver arrangement. Rather than having a separately mounted tweeter and midrange driver, the tweeter in a Uni-Q driver is set into the centre of the midrange.
 This allows for better time alignment and results in the more cohesive sound we hear from current KEF speakers. A simple idea – but it's what sets the company apart from the pack.
 Another successful innovation seen in the latest models is the addition of Metamaterial Absorption Technology (or MAT), which is a small maze-like structure that absorbs 99% of unwanted rearward sound from the back of the tweeter to deliver cleaner, better high frequencies.
 More importantly, KEF has kept pace with the times and diversified into wireless speaker systems alongside passive speakers, with its line of LS wireless all-in-one streaming systems all gaining five-star reviews and setting the standard for speaker systems of this type.
 These products offer a full system without the need for multiple boxes. They also include ample physical connections alongside all the wireless options, making them a great choice if you stream alongside listening to more traditional media like vinyl and CDs.
 How we test stereo speakers 
 Here at What Hi-Fi? we review hundreds of products every year, including no small amount of speakers of all shapes, sizes and types. So how do we come to our review verdicts? And why can you trust them?
 The What Hi-Fi? team has more than 100 years' experience of reviewing, testing and writing about consumer electronics. We have state-of-the-art testing facilities, where our team of expert reviewers do all our in-house testing.
 This gives us complete control over the testing process, ensuring consistency. We always ensure we spend plenty of time with the speakers, trying them with different electronics, in different positions and with different music.
 All products are tested in comparison with rival products in the same category, and all review verdicts are agreed upon by the team as a whole rather than a single reviewer, helping to ensure consistency and avoid individual subjectivity.

 Kickstarter campaign just launched; MSRP is $179 but cheaper now 
 The cassette player revival began with retro-inspired models such as the EDITH WE-001 and FiiO CP13 , but we're beginning to see more modern versions like, well, this strange wall-mounted system . And another new option — the one you're here to read about — definitely falls into the latter camp.
 Coolgeek, whose RGB light-up turntable we covered several months ago, is back with its newest gadget: the P1 Cassette Player.
 Like its turntable, this device is being 'released' on Kickstarter, so you can't buy it immediately. However, from what we've been told, it sounds pretty far along in production, so I don't envision the turn-around time being too long here.

 While the standard price of the P1 is $179 (about £130, AU$260), in true Kickstarter fashion it's available for much cheaper if you sign up to the campaign earlier ; it'll be half that price in the 'Super Early Bird' wave, and slowly increase over time.
 What your money gets you
 (Image credit: CoolkGeek) At its core, Coolgeek's P1 Cassette Player is... well, a cassette player (think Walkman, but Sony makes those), so you don't really need me to run you through what it does, do you? It plays cassettes. But there's more, of course, or we wouldn't be covering it.

 The CD renaissance is going strong, and CD players are looking a little different this time around — here are the quirky disc-spinners you need to see 
 For one, the model has Bluetooth 5.3 connectivity, so you can listen to your tapes using your wireless headphones. There's a 3.5mm jack for wired headphone lovers too, as well as a USB-C port, but the latter's just for charging.
 There's also a little HD display, which is primarily used for arranging the Bluetooth connection. Judging by images we've seen, there's also some colorful LED indicator column (ooh, lights!) probably for volume, but we weren't expressly told what it depicts.

 Plenty of the new cassette players we've seen have playful, pastel-colored designs and curved edges, and Coolgeek's P1 looks a lot more mechanical and industrial in comparison — like true 1970s and 1980s tangible tech.  What if you didn’t have to decide between the best headphones or the best Bluetooth speaker when you’re packing? That’s what the TDM. Neo promises with its hybrid design. This device is creating quite the buzz right now. With Jimmy Fallon declaring it “legendary,” and a decent haul of awards at CES 2026, there’s a reason it turns heads.
 The innovative design twists the headphones into a Bluetooth speaker, and it features impressive battery life. With the right EQ settings through the companion app, the sound quality can be pretty good too.
 However, the price tag is a little steep, the volume is far too quiet, and getting the best positioning for the speaker takes some time. To find out more about the device, keep reading my full TDM. Neo review.

 TDM. Neo review: What I like 
 Quirky design 
 Battery life 
 Sound quality adjustments 
 The TDM. Neo is an interesting device, and there’s a lot to like. The design is a major talking point here, and for good reason — it’s innovative and very useful. The battery life is very impressive, with up to 200 hours of listening in the headphones configuration, and the companion app makes the sound experience even better.
 Quirky design
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) There’s no denying the design of the TDM. Neo turns heads. The headphones transform into a speaker with a simple twist of the headband. They connect with magnets on the side of the headphones so the speaker holds its shape. To listen to your music with headphones instead, you simply unravel the headphones, and the music mode automatically switches. The device weighs 12 ounces, comfortable enough to wear as headphones and to carry around with you as a speaker.
 If you’re pushed for space when packing for a trip, I think the TDM. Neo is the perfect solution. When I’m heading on vacation, I always like to have a speaker with me for my room and a set of headphones for travel, and when trying to pack light, this can prove to be somewhat challenging. I honestly thought this would be just another gimmick, but this headphone/speaker combination is one of the most handy gadgets I’ve ever used.
 Battery life
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) What’s more impressive than the design is the battery life. If you’re using the TDM. Neo as headphones, you’ll get 200 hours of battery life, and if using it as a speaker, you’ll get 16 hours. Obviously, this is a little trickier to put to the test, as I was switching between the modes regularly while using them.

 Other headphones in this price range, such as the Sony WH-1000XM5 , will give you up to 40 hours of listening. The Marshall Milton ANC headphones cost $229 and have upt ot 80 hours of battery life with ANC turned off, so you can find headphones with much higher listening times, meaning the headphones time of the DM. Neo isn’t that impressive, but the speaker time certainly is.
 There is a quick charge option to get eight hours of music playback from five minutes of charge. However, it’s not specified whether this is for the headphones or the speaker mode. The battery module is also replaceable, meaning you’re less likely to have to replace the full unit down the line.
 Sound quality with app
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Is this the best sound quality of any headphones or speaker I’ve used? Absolutely not. However, the TDM. Neo’s companion app lets you adjust the EQ settings to make the sound much more balanced. To use the custom EQ feature, you need to create an account, or you can choose from one of the six pre-programmed EQs. I used Qobuz , our pick for the best music streaming service for audiophiles, to listen to music with the speaker and headphones.
 During my testing, I created an EQ with increased bass and decreased treble. The high-frequency sounds were a bit tinny, so decreasing the treble made the sound much better. I listened to “Roman Holiday” by Fontaines D.C., which is a guitar-heavy track. It generally sounded good, but even with adjustments, the treble sounded a little tinny and clipped. This is fine for casual listening but makes the soundstage feel narrow. But the bass in this song was impressive and guided the rhythm of the track.
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) I also listened to “If I Get High” by Nothing But Thieves. This track starts off stripped back and slow, with the vocals as the focus. The vocals sounded amazing and clear here, but as the song built, we were met with the tininess again as the drums and cymbals kicked in. Again, the bass guitar shone here, making the sound much fuller.
 Finally, I listened to “Witches” by Alice Phoebe Lou, which features shimmering sounds that carried very well, and actually avoided any tinny sounds at all. The vocals here are very delicate, but they were replicated well through the speaker.
 I found the sound quality much better as a speaker when the device is in the carry case, as this acts as sound dampening, so the higher frequencies don’t sound as harsh.
 TDM. Neo review: What I don’t like 
 Pricing 
 Too quiet 
 It has to be positioned perfectly 
 Although I mostly like the TDM. Neo, and I love how innovative the design is, there are a few things that are a little annoying. The price tag seems steep; it doesn’t get loud enough, and it needs that Goldilocks positioning to get the sound just right .
 Price tag
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The first thing I don’t like about this device is the price tag. The TDM. Neo is available for $249 /£249 from the TDM. online store , but for this price, I would expect premium sound and build, which I don’t feel I got. The sound is certainly good, but is it $250-good? I don’t think so. Instead, you’re getting a budget pair of headphones and a budget speaker but paying for both devices — you’re paying for the convenience of a two-in-one product.
 In terms of quality, I’d liken the speaker to cheaper options like the Tozo PE1 , which costs $39. But for around the same price as the TDM. you could get the JBL Charge 6 ($199) that has 28 hours of battery life and louder volume.
 If you consider headphones, $249 places you firmly in the premium category. The Marshall Milton headphones cost $229 and have a powerful bass performance, so if the headphones feature on the Neos is what you’ll use most, you should get the Miltons.
 Volume
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The TDM. Neo doesn’t actually get very loud in headphones or speaker mode. When I’m using a speaker, I want to blast my music throughout my whole house, but the sound just doesn't carry.
 For massive sound from a small speaker, I’d recommend the Bose SoundLink Micro 2 ($129). This speaker has sound that carries easily and bass that booms when you need it to.
 Speaker positioning
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) How good the TDM. Neo sounds is highly dependent on its positioning. This is the case for a lot of speakers, but with the twisting nature of the Neo, it’s more important to make sure it’s sat just right. The sound comes from two speakers on either side of where the headphone earcups are folded, so it can’t be placed flat on the table — although this feels most natural. Instead, it needs to be balanced on its side so both speakers are exposed.
 This balancing act can feel precarious at times, but with the carry case for the speaker to sit in, you can clip it to something so it’s not touching any surfaces. This is how you’ll get the best sound.
 TDM. Neo compared 
 Though I’ve made comparisons to other headphones and speakers throughout this review, it’s not exactly a fair competition. The TDM. Neo gives you the opportunity to have two devices in one, in theory saving some cash, but in doing so, both devices compromise on their overall quality.
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) With that said, there are a few similar devices on the market, but they’re not as polished as the TDM. version of the device. The HyperGear Flip ($34) headphones have earcups that flip outward to act as external speakers, but the design of the Neo is what makes it so functional.
 Who should buy the TDM. Neo? 
 I think there is a place for the TDM. Neo in most people’s audio setup. The highly innovative design means you get two devices in one, and this is incredibly useful if you’re trying to pack light while traveling. The battery life is impressive too, and you can get good sound quality by making some adjustments in the companion app.
 However, I personally think the price tag is a little steep for the quality you’re getting, and the speaker volume doesn’t go high enough for my liking. It’s also annoying that the speaker has to be perfectly balanced to get the best sound, although the carry case and strap make this easier.
 Do I think the hybrid device is perfect? No. But do I think we’re now going to see more hybrid audio devices follow in its footsteps? Absolutely!

THE 6 BEST CD PLAYERS WITH BLUETOOTH
by Shane /
Last updated 3 November 2026
GUIDES, GUIDES, HIFI

Table of Contents

Have you been looking for a CD player with Bluetooth connectivity, so you can both listen to your CDs and stream with ease from your smartphone? Well, here are six of my favourite CD players that bring both CD playback and Bluetooth connectivity together.

Before we get started, it’s important to note that Bluetooth is a rare feature for CD players alone. So, many of these CD players are all-in-one systems like the Eversolo Play and Naim Uniti Star, but don’t think that makes them any less capable. These use fantastic DACs, which is what matters with high fidelity audio playback

We also have options like the Technics SL-G700M2E-K, which bring all the streaming features you could desire. So, let’s dive into the best CD players with Bluetooth – from dedicated CD players to all-in-one systems.

IN A HURRY?

Denon CEOL RCD-N10 Network CD Music System	This is a little powerhouse of a product with great connectivity and a cool exterior.	Check current price
Marantz Melody X M-CR612 All-In-One Hi-Fi System	One of the best-looking solutions for its size. Packs in more features than you think.	Check current price
Technics SA-C600 Network CD Receiver	Elevating what sound should be like from an all-in-one system. Often misunderstood, this is one of the best there is.	Check current price
SHOP CD PLAYERS WITH BLUETOOTH
WHY WE’VE CHOSEN THESE CD PLAYERS

CD players with Bluetooth might sound like an easy find, but in truth, it isn’t, which you’ll know all too well, seeing as you’ve arrived on this page! It’s usually the amplifier which includes the Bluetooth connectivity.

However, we’ve found one option that is particularly well-suited to those looking for a standalone unit, while the rest are ideal as all-in-one solutions, offering everything you might need.

To choose the players for this list, I looked at their connectivity and how it performed in a typical room without pushing it too hard. For a fair evaluation, I tested the players with the same speakers, the Q Acoustics Q 5020, using tracks by AC/DC, B.B. King, M83, and Womack & Womack on CDs.

All these systems performed exceedingly well for their price point, and I actually managed to find the limit of the Q Acoustics Q 5020 speakers with the last two systems!

I then tried the same songs via Bluetooth and one song via AirPlay, just to see if there was a difference

I also wanted to walk you through the inputs and outputs, along with any features I felt were worth highlighting. What you’ll find in this article is the result of that process: a brief walkthrough of six CD players with Bluetooth connectivity for smartphones.

THE BEST CD PLAYERS WITH BLUETOOTH
1. DENON CEOL RCD-N10 NETWORK CD MUSIC SYSTEM

Key features

65W per channel
Supports multiple streaming platforms
Hands-free with Amazon Alexa

Pros

Minimalist design will suit many setups
Includes subwoofer output for upgraded bass
Simple to set up

Cons

No DAB tuner

The Denon CEOL RCD-N10 Network CD Music System is cool, compact, and very easy to use, and it makes the top of our list for good reason.

Immediately on unpacking, I was struck by just how compact the system is, measuring 280mm wide, 305mm in depth, and just 108mm in height. There is also a plethora of connections and features.

Its streaming features include all the big hitters like TIDAL, Spotify, and TuneIn; plus, its ability to play hi-res audio is a nice touch, as not all do.

Looking at the connections, at the rear, you get both digital and optical inputs, plus an FM aerial input. On the front, you get a 3.5mm headphone jack, a neatly designed display just below the CD drawer, and two buttons on either side, plus a USB input.

The main controls are located on the top, which keeps the front of the Denon so clean-looking. These are touch-sensitive and give you all the simple requirements needed to operate the Denon CEOL, while the remote control gives you even more.

Plugging a pair of Q Acoustics Q 5020 bookshelf speakers from our system builder made use of the 65 watts of power on tap, and playing a selection of CDs instantly presented the system’s musical presence.

It was easy to connect to the network, while streaming to the CD player with Bluetooth from my smartphone was even easier. Playing Spotify via AirPlay 2 was just a couple of clicks away, too.

FIND OUT MORE
2. MARANTZ MELODY X M-CR612 ALL-IN-ONE HI-FI SYSTEM

Key features

HEOS app control
Includes voice assist
Multiple streaming options

Pros

Elegant design
Warm, musical sound
Works well with a wide range of speakers

Cons

It can sound a little weak with bass on Bluetooth

The Marantz Melody X M-CR612 All-In-One Hi-Fi System has to be one of the best-looking on this list, thanks to that classic Marantz Design. And it only misses out on the top spot because it requires you to be a little more tech-savvy with its setup.

Like the Denon above, the Marantz Melody is almost identical in its proportions. It’s already unboxed in our showroom, so if you’re in the Bacup area, take a look!

From the front, the classic Marantz design is present, and the buttons feel very satisfying and precise to use, showing Marantz’s dedication to quality in every detail.

At the rear, there are two pairs of speaker outputs, allowing you to either bi-wire or use the Marantz to play music in a second zone. A subwoofer output is also available for zone 1, along with a DAB/FM tuner aerial, two digital optical Toslink ports, a single stereo RCA input, and both Ethernet and USB inputs. There’s an analogue output, too, which is a nice touch.

Powering the unit on and playing my first track revealed a far more grown-up, musical feel to the sound, bringing a warm tone through the speakers.

It’s fairly simple to stream music to this CD player via Bluetooth. That Marantz sound remains, although the bass does fall away a little, which isn’t uncommon for Bluetooth streaming. It’s easy to understand why many choose the Marantz Melody as it’s an ideal CD player, can stream music via Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, and has multiple streaming services.

FIND OUT MORE
3. TECHNICS SA-C600 NETWORK CD RECEIVER

Key features

MM turntable connectivity
Hi-res streaming capabilities
Refined power system

Pros

Bags of power for driving floor-standing speakers
Premium build quality
The interactive disc loading system is a nice touch

Cons

Not as aesthetically pleasing as others on the list

Another popular CD player system, the Technics SA-C600 Network CD Receiver boasts double the wattage of the Marantz above, and you can instantly tell.

This is a very popular CD receiver, so it’s also out in our showroom, if you fancy a look.

First, let’s discuss the remote. It’s weighty, and its buttons are clearly placed. It actually feels a bit like the flagship Panasonic TV remote, which, if you know, you’ll understand, as there is a link between the two brands.

On the system itself, you’ll notice there is no CD drawer. Rather, you’ll find a rather cool transparent swivel disc on top. It gives the SA-C600 a unique touch of class, and upon use, it feels as though you’re interacting with vinyl.

At the rear, you’ll find a dedicated phono stage, separate line-in, both digital and coaxial inputs, a USB-B PC input, and a subwoofer out. Let’s not forget the DAB/FM aerial or Ethernet inputs either.

Using the Q Acoustics Q 5020 speakers, I was impressed by the large soundstage that makes full use of the speakers. It’s the same story when using the Technics SA-C600 with Bluetooth, and thanks to its high-quality built-in DAC, it can sample those lesser quality Bluetooth streams and make them stand out from the norm.

If you want more musicality, I recommend using the SA-C600 with a pair of Technics speakers.

FIND OUT MORE
4. EVERSOLO PLAY STREAMING AMPLIFIER CD EDITION

Key features

60W of digital power
CD player enables ripping too
Roon Ready

Pros

Modern touch screen colour display
App control is intuitive
Probably one of the best products of 2025

Cons

CD player section feels a bit flimsy

As a newcomer to the market, the Eversolo Play Streaming Amplifier CD Edition is creating a bit of a stir. I had a demo unit to play with, and hooking it to a pair of Q Acoustics Q 5020 bookshelf speakers was simple.

Taking a look a the rear, you can see there’s a plethora of connections – far more than any of the other products in this lineup, with it only missing USB-B and USB-C for PC connectivity. But HDMI is an option as it has ARC.

From the front, you can tell this isn’t like any of the other electronics in this lineup, as you are presented with a large 5.5-inch colour display touch screen. There’s a plethora of app icons like TIDAL, Qobuz, and Amazon Music, and to the side, there’s a large dial that controls both power on/off and volume.

The CD player section is located on the left-hand side of the unit. It feels a bit flimsy, but for functionality, and the sheer size of the unit, it’s a marvel that they have even managed to package a CD player into it.

Streaming-wise, there’s the standard Bluetooth 5.3 for superior audio playback.

Really, this player/amplifier is a new generation of electronics. Streaming, archiving, playing DSD or even to DOP64… it can do a lot! Oh, and it doesn’t sound too bad either.

FIND OUT MORE
5. NAIM UNITI STAR AUDIOPHILE ALL-IN-ONE MUSIC SYSTEM

Key features

HDMI ARC connectivity
Plethora of streaming options
Custom-designed toroidal transformer

Pros

Sleek design
Cool volume control that feels exquisite
There isn’t much it cannot do

Cons

High price point

The only other system with a colour display in this lineup is the Naim Uniti Star Audiophile All-in-One Music System. It’s priced significantly higher than the Eversolo Play, but when you compare the two, you can tell that the Uniti Star is a very different beast.

Plugging the Q Acoustics Q 5020 feels like we are short-changing the Naim, but as this is a fair test, this is what we’re going with, taking these speakers as far as they can musically.

At the rear, it feels so much less cluttered with inputs than other systems, but don’t be fooled into thinking it has less. The Uniti Star is a full-sized system compared to the rest, enabling it to be better set out in a far cleaner way, and it even includes an SD card slot which none of the other have.

Ot the front, the CD player is neatly hidden on the left. The right-hand side is where you’ll find that colour display with control features and a USB and headphone jack. On top, you’ll notice the volume dial, which is up to Rolls-Royce standards for tactile touch.

Like the Eversolo, almost every conceivable streaming service is available, and it’s Roon-ready and includes Chromecast Audio. It accepts just about every musical format you can list, while also supporting Bluetooth 5.3 for CD-quality playback.

Nothing really comes close to what the Naim has to offer, but that price is premium. For those who dare to own it, they will never look elsewhere, as nothing really competes with it.

FIND OUT MORE
6. TECHNICS SL-G700M2E-K NETWORK/SUPER AUDIO CD PLAYER

Key features

Universal CD/SACD Player
High Precision Coherent D/A Converter
Dual mono-configured ESS ES9026PRO DACs

Pros

Great sound
Fantastic array of connectivity options
Build quality matches its price point

Cons

Display lets it down

The Technics SL-G700M2E-K Network/Super Audio CD Player is one of just a few dedicated CD players to include Bluetooth.

This is ideal if you have an established separates system; its perfect partner would be the Technics SU-G700M2.

At the rear, there are more connections than you might think, with three digital inputs, including a USB-B PC input and an Ethernet LAN connection, and two wifi antennas. Its outputs also include optical and coaxial digital outputs, while the analogue boasts both RCA and balanced XLR.

On the front, there are the buttons as you would expect to find on a CD player, like eject, play, and pause, but as this CD player offers more, you also get a dial control with additional buttons, which also includes headphone out volume control.

Unlike most CD players, the SL-G700M2E-K supports a comprehensive streaming platform, matching the rest of this lineup with TIDAL, Qobuz, and Spotify. There’s also SACD playback. meaning it’s a true universal CD player.

Bluetooth streaming from your smartphone enables you to take full advantage of those dual mono-configured ESS ES9026PRO DACs built in, while streaming via AirPlay 2 allows for even more detail when resolutions are higher.

As CD players go, this feels like quite a unique product, and the fact that it also includes a full-size 6.35mm headphone jack means you can use it on its own without anything other than a nice pair of headphones or speakers.

FIND OUT MORE
HOW TO CHOOSE THE BEST CD PLAYER WITH BLUETOOTH

To choose the right Bluetooth CD player for you, you need to think about how you’re going to use it. If your streaming files are MP3 or lossy and you just want to stream music from your smartphone, you need to look out for these particular logos. SBC, AAC, and aptX are certifiable musical streaming formats which both your smartphone and Bluetooth streamer need to be compatible with in order to play music via this option.

For CD quality and compatibility, aptX Lossless or aptX HD are a further requirement. There are other options like LDAC and aptX Adaptive, depending on the platform you’re streaming from.

After you’ve narrowed these things down, the choices become a lot easier. You’ll then need to decide on aesthetics, sound quality, and budget. If you already own speakers, most of the systems on our list will be suitable; just be sure to check that both will allow for seamless integration.

FAQS
IS BLUETOOTH AS GOOD AS CD QUALITY?

In order to match or even better Bluetooth streaming than that of CD quality, you have to look out for the aptX and aptX HD logos, as aptX matches CD quality, while aptX HD can exceed it.

CAN YOU PLAY REGULAR CDS ON A BLUETOOTH CD PLAYER?

You can play regular CDs on a Bluetooth CD player. Bluetooth is an extra feature that allows you to also stream your music.

WHAT DOES MP3 MEAN ON A CD PLAYER?

If you see the MP3 logo on a CD player, this means that you might be able to stream the music format MP3 via Bluetooth or USB, or record to compatible CD-R/CD-RW discs.

FINAL THOUGHTS

If you’ve been searching for the best CD player with Bluetooth, I hope you’ve found one on our list of six! If you would rather stream from your CD player using Bluetooth, I recommend the FiiO DM13; this is a gem of a portable CD player. But other than that, our well-rounded list above should have you covered.

 Put the headphones or earbuds into explicit pairing mode.
 Select CD mode on the player.
 Activate the player’s Bluetooth transmit or search function.
 Keep the devices close during first pairing.
 Wait for the connection confirmation, then start the disc.
 For the JENSEN, the manual describes a dedicated Bluetooth-transmit search process and recommends keeping the target device close during initial pairing. If pairing fails, power-cycle both devices and repeat the process.
 Most inexpensive transmitters pair with one Bluetooth audio device at a time, although the exact limit must be verified. Wireless headphones also need their own charge. Bluetooth can add audio delay, which is usually irrelevant for music but noticeable with video.
 Using one in a car
 A transmitting player can work with a car that has Bluetooth media-audio reception. The car may need to initiate pairing from its own menu, and it must not already be connected to another phone. Some systems support Bluetooth only for calls, not music.

 If the car has a 3.5-mm auxiliary input, use the CD player’s wired output. If it has only USB, do not assume that port accepts live audio; many USB ports provide power or read files rather than acting as an analog audio input. A separate Bluetooth receiver or FM adapter may be necessary.
 Troubleshooting common failures
 Bluetooth pairing fails
 Fully charge both devices.
 Disconnect nearby phones and speakers.
 Put the headphones or speaker into pairing mode, not merely powered-on mode.
 Enter the CD player’s transmit/search mode.
 Keep the devices close.
 Restart both devices and try again.
 Test wired headphones. If wired playback works, the CD mechanism is probably fine and the problem is pairing or compatibility.
 Audio cuts out while walking
 Check whether anti-skip is enabled, clean the disc, inspect the lid and disc fit, and recharge the player. Test wired headphones: if wired playback also skips, the cause is mechanical, the disc, or the battery—not Bluetooth. Even a large anti-skip buffer is not a guarantee during severe movement.
 It works with headphones but not the car
 Confirm that the car supports Bluetooth media audio rather than hands-free calling only. Remove competing phone connections and follow the car’s pairing procedure. A Bluetooth transmitter cannot pair directly with another transmitter.
 The product has Bluetooth but cannot send CD audio
 This is usually a direction mismatch. The player may be a Bluetooth receiver designed for phone streaming. Return to the product documentation and look specifically for transmit or output language.
 Are older Sony, Philips, or Panasonic players worth buying?
 They can be, especially when replaceable batteries, a sturdy mechanism, or a known 3.5-mm output matters more than built-in Bluetooth. But an older player still needs a separate transmitter for wireless listening, and condition varies widely. Check that the lid closes firmly, the disc spins consistently, the headphone jack is clean, the battery compartment has no corrosion, and the seller accepts returns.
 A used player is not automatically more durable, and a marketplace listing is not evidence of long-term reliability. For the simplest setup, a documented new transmitter-equipped player is easier. For repairability and AA operation, the older-player route can be more attractive.

 Buy the JENSEN CD-60R-BT if you want the clearest documented path from a physical CD to Bluetooth headphones, earbuds, a speaker, or a compatible car stereo. Choose a boombox such as the iLive IBC233B if your priority is built-in sound and phone streaming. Choose an AA-powered player plus a separate transmitter if replaceable batteries and modular repairs matter more than one-device convenience.  How to Choose the Best Bluetooth CD Player for Your Home Stereo
 Choosing a Bluetooth CD player for home stereo use comes down to five questions: room size, codec support, source variety, power needs, and integration with your existing setup. Let me walk through each one based on what I learned during three months of testing.
 What room size are you filling?
 For a bedroom, den, or office under 200 square feet, 18 to 30 watts is plenty. The Philips Micro Music 18W and LONPOO LP-886 both handle that range well. For medium rooms between 200 and 350 square feet, look for 60 to 100W systems like the Panasonic SC-PM700PP-K or Philips TAM8905. For large open living rooms above 350 square feet, the PHILIPS FX10 at 230W is the safer pick.
 Do you care about Bluetooth codec quality?
 The Bluetooth codec you use matters more than most buyers realize. SBC, which is the default on every Bluetooth CD player, compresses audio and removes some detail. AAC is better, especially for iPhone users. aptX and aptX HD retain more of the original signal, and LDAC pushes quality even further. If codec quality matters to you, the Philips Bluetooth 5.4 system with Auracast is the only model on this list that supports modern codecs out of the box.
 How many sources do you actually need?
 I tested each system with CD, CD-R, CD-RW, MP3 CD, USB, FM, aux, and Bluetooth. The Philips TAM8905 is the only model that adds Wi-Fi, Spotify Connect, and internet radio on top of all of that. If you want one box that does everything, the TAM8905 is the clear winner. If you mostly play CDs and stream from your phone, almost any system on this list will work.
 Do you need optical input for a TV?
 Only the Aiwa Exos includes an optical digital input. If you want to use your CD player as a TV soundbase, that one feature eliminates every other option on this list. Otherwise, plan to use HDMI ARC on your TV or a separate soundbar.
 Will it integrate with your existing stereo?
 All eight systems on this list are self-contained shelf systems with built-in speakers. None of them have preamp outputs for connecting to a separate amplifier or powered speakers. If you already own a high-end amplifier and floor-standing speakers, you will need a dedicated network CD player without Bluetooth speakers instead.
 What about Bluetooth vs wired sound quality?
 Direct CD playback through a quality DAC always sounds better than Bluetooth streaming from your phone, because Bluetooth compresses the audio. That said, modern aptX and LDAC codecs come surprisingly close to CD quality. For casual listening, Bluetooth is more than good enough. For critical listening sessions with the lights down, switch to physical CD.
 Frequently Asked Questions About CD Players with Bluetooth
 What is the best CD player with Bluetooth?
 The PHILIPS FX10 is the best overall Bluetooth CD player for home stereo use in 2026. It combines a powerful 230W dual-amplifier output with reliable Bluetooth streaming, and it has more than 2,800 verified reviews. For tighter budgets, the LONPOO LP-886 delivers surprising quality under $100.
 Can you play regular CDs on a Bluetooth CD player?
 Yes. Every Bluetooth CD player on this list plays standard CD, CD-R, and CD-RW discs without any issue. Bluetooth is an additional input option for streaming audio from your phone, not a replacement for the disc drive. Your existing CD collection will play exactly as it always has.
 Which CD player has the best sound quality?
 The Philips TAM8905 had the best sound quality in my testing thanks to its 100W output, real 5.25-inch woofers, and dome tweeters. The PHILIPS FX10 came a close second with louder but slightly less refined sound. Both significantly outperform the budget options for serious listening.
 What is the best Bluetooth receiver for home stereo?
 If you want a full shelf system rather than a separate receiver, the Philips TAM8905 with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth is the most complete option. If you already own an amplifier and only need a Bluetooth receiver, you would need a standalone Bluetooth adapter instead, since none of the systems in this guide have preamp outputs.
 Final Verdict
 After three months of testing, eight Bluetooth-enabled CD players, and hundreds of discs and playlists, I keep coming back to three winners. The PHILIPS FX10 is the best CD player with Bluetooth for most people who want big, room-filling sound and proven reliability. The Philips TAM8905 is the best premium pick if you also want Wi-Fi streaming and internet radio. The LONPOO LP-886 is the best budget Bluetooth CD player under $100, and it surprised me with how well it competes with systems twice its price.
 Whatever you choose from this list, you will end up with a CD player with Bluetooth for home stereo use that bridges your disc collection and modern streaming without forcing you to pick one over the other. For 2026, any of these eight will serve you well, and our team stands behind the recommendations based on real listening time, not just spec sheets.

 Key Buying Factors for Cd Players with Bluetooth 
 Bluetooth Function
 Check whether Bluetooth is designed for receiving audio from a phone, transmitting CD audio to wireless headphones or speakers, or both. “Bluetooth” alone does not always mean the player supports every connection type.
 Built-In Speakers and Sound
 Portable units with integrated stereo speakers are convenient, but larger home systems generally provide stronger volume and fuller sound. Look for bass and treble controls, speaker size, and any stated power rating if audio quality is a priority.
 Power and Portability
 Rechargeable batteries are useful for flexible placement, while AC-powered systems are better for fixed listening. Consider battery capacity, charging method, handle design, and whether the player can operate while charging.
 Extra Playback Options
 FM radio, USB playback, headphone support, LCD displays, remote controls, and FM transmission can add versatility. Choose only the features that fit your routine, since extra functions may increase size or complexity.
 Controls and Compatibility
 Confirm supported disc types, button layout, display readability, skip and repeat controls, and whether the unit resumes playback after interruption. For car use, verify that FM transmission ranges and power accessories suit your vehicle.
